prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock: the magic-wavelength lattice that lets many atoms be interrogated free of Doppler and recoil shifts, and its realisation at fractional uncertainties of 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks (B015) as a stand-alone prize to Katori and Ye, and the first-round exchange has sharpened rather than weakened the case. In answer to the chair's question on novelty: the 2005 prize gave the optical frequency comb as the counter, and the 2012 prize gave control and measurement of single trapped quantum systems, with ion clocks as one outcome. What is new is the magic-wavelength lattice, in which the light shifts of the two clock levels cancel by design, so that thousands of neutral atoms are held Doppler- and recoil-free and interrogated in parallel. That removes the old trade-off between atom number and motional shifts, it is why the statistical stability allowed 10^-18 systematic evaluation in hours rather than months, and neither earlier citation covers it. The evidence is the kind I trust: independent clocks at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE agree in direct comparison, and the same instruments already measure gravitational redshift across millimetres, bound drifts of constants and search for dark matter. Draft citation, as requested: 'for the optical lattice clock: the magic-wavelength lattice that lets many atoms be interrogated free of Doppler and recoil shifts, and its realisation at fractional uncertainties of 10^-18'. It names the scheme and the regime, does not mention the second's redefinition, and does not claim combs or ion clocks. On the redefinition, I would treat it as timing only and keep it out of the citation. Waiting a year would not change the scientific record, which is already in hand, and the pending redefinition would then be a consequence of the achievement and not a condition for recognising it. Credit is a clean two-name pair; no other shortlisted configuration offers that with this level of reproduction.
statement.case_against: The objections I take most seriously have not gone away. First, lineage: a sceptical reader can still say that going from 10^-15 to 10^-18 is a large quantitative step on the 2005 and 2012 foundations, and that the statute's emphasis on discovery or invention is met more obviously by a new phenomenon (B017, B051). My answer is that the lattice scheme is an invention in the statutory sense and that the clocks produce measurements of nature, but I accept that members who weigh a new state of matter higher will reasonably differ. Second, credit: Lemonde, Pfau, Lemke, Ludlow and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups made decisive contributions to making lattice clocks work, and naming only Katori and Ye leaves them out. I have no alternative pair to propose and I do not think a three-name version would be more accurate, since the field was built by many groups. Third, a recognised weakness in my own position is that I am not in a position to audit early lattice-clock priority myself, and an external reviewer's report on that would be welcome.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the ion-clock lineage is the real difficulty and that the citation must stress the lattice concept and the large number of atoms, which Katori and Ye did and Wineland did not. She and I were asked by the chair to draft the wording.
responses.response: I agree, and I have written the citation that way: it names the magic-wavelength lattice and the many-atom, motion-free interrogation, and then the 10^-18 regime, and nothing about combs, single ions or the second. I would add one point from the experimental side to your list of what had to be understood: the 10^-18 evaluation depended on blackbody-radiation shift control and on cavity-stabilised lasers whose stability allowed the lattice clock's many-atom averaging to be exploited. Those are Ye's group's contributions, and they are why the pair is Katori for the scheme and Ye for the regime. If you prefer 'optical lattice clocks' before the explanatory clause I have no objection; the point is that the lattice and the 10^-18 level both appear.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B015 seventh and holds that it is a new level of precision rather than a new principle, but now says he would support B015 if the topological insulator attribution cannot be resolved.
responses.response: I think the credit question you describe for B051 will not resolve inside three names: Mele cannot easily be separated from Kane, and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal that guided Molenkamp is outside any trio, with Zhang deceased. That is not a fault in the physics, and I agree your discovery case is secure and reproduced. But it means B051 enters the final ballot with an unfairness that B015 does not carry. On your principle objection I would put it concretely: the lattice does something an ion trap cannot, because with ions one cannot interrogate thousands of atoms at once without Coulomb shifts, and with free neutral atoms one cannot avoid Doppler and recoil. The magic-wavelength condition solves both at the same time. I hope you will treat B015 as acceptable now, rather than only if B051 fails.

responses.point: Olsson prefers magic-angle graphene (B017) but accepts the maturity concern and the unresolved credit for Cao and the Dean, Young, Efetov and Yacoby groups, and says she would not oppose B015 if the committee prefers a metrology prize, provided the citation names the invention (the lattice clock).
responses.response: Your condition is met by my draft, which names the lattice clock and the magic-wavelength scheme and does not rest on precision alone. On discovery versus refinement, I would say the clocks are also a discovery tool: millimetre-scale redshift in one sample and bounds on constants are measurements of nature that were not possible before. I do not dismiss B017, and the prediction-then-experiment structure is attractive. My hesitation, which you share, is that the mechanism of the superconductivity is open and twist-angle disorder makes sample dependence a real issue, whereas lattice-clock comparisons between laboratories have already closed the question of reproducibility. I would put B017 a few years ahead of where it is now, not behind.

responses.point: Danielsson now prefers a two-part prize pairing B015 with B040 (IceCube, Halzen alone), giving Katori, Ye and Halzen, on the ground that both are cases where an instrument was built to read a clue from nature, and concedes that single-name credit for IceCube is the weak point.
responses.response: I share the principle, since building the instrument that reads nature is exactly what I value, and the diffuse flux since 2013 is firm. But I would not add B040 now, for two reasons. The credit: a single name for a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA, Baikal and ANTARES behind it, is the weakest attribution on the shortlist, and no second or third name has been put forward that the three-person limit could absorb. The maturity: the source identifications (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, the Galactic plane) are still at moderate significance and developing, so a citation to neutrino astronomy would be easier to defend later. A weak second part would also carry the first part into a vulnerable configuration, when B015 stands well alone. If an expert report produces a defensible credit within the limit, I would reconsider it for a later year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts an invention in precision measurement as prize-level given the 2005 and 2012 precedents; this is a matter of weighting that I cannot settle with data.

Whether early contributors outside Katori and Ye (Lemonde, Pfau, Lemke, Ludlow and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups) would be seen as unfairly excluded; I do not have an independent priority record and would welcome an expert report.
Whether waiting for the redefinition of the second would improve the standing of the prize; I judge it as timing only but cannot rule out that other members read it differently.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: during my PhD I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Jun Ye's JILA group belongs to the same Boulder precision-spectroscopy tradition. I have no direct collaboration, co-authorship or financial tie with Katori or Ye, and I regard this as a scientific lineage, not a conflict that requires recusal, but I ask that it remain on record, as the chair noted. I am in the WACQT management team, which touches circuit QED (B012) only indirectly, and B012 is no longer one of my alternatives. I am also a member of Deep Light Vision AB's management; that company works on ultrasound optical tomography and has no connection to any shortlisted candidate. I have no other conflict.
